content: Chorioamnionitis is an inflammatory condition that occurs during pregnancy, primarily affecting the uterus. It is caused by a bacterial infection of the amniotic sac and the surrounding amniotic fluid. This condition poses significant risks to both the mother and the fetus and is recognized as the leading cause of premature labor. Chorioamnionitis can be classified into subtypes based on the patient’s clinical presentation, the type of infiltrating immune cells, the anatomical regions infiltrated by neutrophils (staging), and the intensity of inflammation (grading). It is an inflammatory disorder of the fetal membranes, most commonly resulting from an infectious etiology. A characteristic gross pathological finding is the opaque appearance of the fetal membranes. Microscopically, neutrophilic infiltration of the amniotic cavity and/or the chorionic plate is a hallmark feature. The condition can be caused by bacterial, fungal, or viral microorganisms. It is essential to differentiate chorioamnionitis from other conditions that may present with maternal fever, abdominal pain, or maternal/fetal tachycardia. For example, epidural-related fever should be considered in patients with epidural anesthesia who develop low-grade fever without tachycardia during labor. Extrauterine infections should be suspected in patients with fever and abdominal pain, while noninfectious conditions like placental abruption should be considered in cases of abdominal pain without fever. The global prevalence of chorioamnionitis is estimated to be approximately 4,000 cases per 100,000 individuals. It is more commonly observed in individuals under 18 years of age. Gestational age is a strong predictor, with higher prevalence in those delivering between 21 and 24 weeks of gestation. Male infants are more frequently affected than females. The condition is also more common among individuals of Hispanic and Asian/Pacific Islander descent. Risk factors for developing chorioamnionitis include preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), prematurity, nulliparity, prolonged labor and rupture of membranes, multiple digital vaginal examinations, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, internal fetal monitoring, epidural anesthesia, immunocompromised states, maternal behavioral conditions, and infections. Clinical findings associated with chorioamnionitis include maternal fever, uterine tenderness, purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid, and maternal/fetal tachycardia. Fetal complications may include preterm birth, neonatal sepsis, neurological complications, and respiratory complications. Maternal complications can include cesarean section, postpartum hemorrhage, and other sequelae. There is no single diagnostic test for chorioamnionitis. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and/or histopathological evaluation. Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed based on features such as maternal fever, uterine tenderness, maternal/fetal tachycardia, and foul-smelling or purulent amniotic fluid. The gold standard for diagnosis is a microbiological culture of the amniotic fluid. Physical examination findings often include fever, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, tachycardia, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Laboratory findings may include positive amniotic fluid cultures, bacteria or white blood cells on Gram stain, decreased glucose levels, and elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels. Histological findings include neutrophilic infiltration of the chorioamniotic membranes. There are no specific findings on electrocardiogram (ECG), X-ray, or ultrasound directly associated with chorioamnionitis. However, ultrasound may be useful in identifying complications such as postpartum hemorrhage, pelvic abscesses, endomyometritis, intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, respiratory distress syndrome, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Similarly, CT scans and MRIs do not show direct findings of chorioamnionitis but may help diagnose complications like pelvic infections, abscesses, adrenal abscesses, subphrenic abscesses, spontaneous preterm delivery, white matter injury, and intraventricular hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) may aid in detecting neuroinflammation in histologic chorioamnionitis and assessing motor and cognitive development in affected infants. Treatment of chorioamnionitis involves antimicrobial therapy, with the preferred regimen being a combination of ampicillin and gentamicin. Supportive therapies, such as antipyretics, may also be used. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing chorioamnionitis. Primary prevention strategies include inducing labor after 34 weeks of gestation and administering prophylactic antimicrobial therapy in cases of PPROM. There are no established measures for secondary prevention of chorioamnionitis.
